To defraud someone means to deliberately trick or deceive them in order to take something valuable away from them — usually money, property, or a legal right they are entitled to.

Think of it as a combination of two things happening at the same time:

  • You lie to someone (or hide the truth from them)
  • And because of that lie, they lose something while you gain something

Both parts must happen together. A lie alone is not defrauding. A loss alone is not defrauding. It is specifically the act of using deception as a tool to cause that loss.
Breaking It Down: The Three Pillars

Every act of defrauding has three essential ingredients:

1. Deception — You say something false, hide the truth, or create a misleading picture of reality. This could be a spoken lie, a written lie, a forged document, a fake identity, or even just staying silent about something you were obligated to reveal.

2. Intent — The deception is deliberate. You are not making an honest mistake. You know the truth, and you are choosing to hide or distort it. This is what separates defrauding from simply being wrong.

3. Deprivation — The victim loses something of value as a direct result of your deception. They were robbed — not physically, but through manipulation of their mind and trust. They gave up something because you made them believe a false reality.
What Can Someone Be Defrauded Of?

The "something valuable" that is taken can be many things:

  • Money (the most common — e.g., you pay someone for something that doesn't exist)
  • Property (e.g., a house, a car, goods)
  • Services (e.g., free labour, professional work obtained dishonestly)
  • Legal rights or benefits (e.g., insurance payouts, government benefits, inheritance)
  • Personal information that has financial or legal value

Example 1 — The Fake Seller:
A person posts an advertisement online selling a car that doesn't exist. You send them the money. They disappear. You have been defrauded. They deceived you (fake car), you lost something (your money), and they gained something (your money). All three pillars are present.

Example 2 — The Lying Employee:
An employee submits fake receipts to their company claiming they spent money on business travel, when they actually stayed home. The company pays them back. The employee has defrauded the company — they lied about expenses to take money that was not owed to them.

Example 3 — The False Doctor:
Someone pretends to be a licensed doctor and charges patients for medical consultations. The patients are defrauded — they paid for something (a real medical service from a qualified professional) that was not what they actually received.

Example 4 — Insurance Fraud:
A person deliberately damages their own car and then tells the insurance company it was an accident, in order to receive a payout. They have defrauded the insurance company.

Example 5 — Investor Fraud:
A businessman tells investors that their money will be used to build a profitable factory. In reality, no factory is ever built, and he uses the money for himself. He has defrauded the investors.

Defrauding is not limited to individuals tricking other individuals. It can happen across many relationships:

  • A person can defraud another person
  • A person can defraud a company
  • A company can defraud its customers or investors
  • A person can defraud the government (e.g., lying on a tax return to pay less tax, or falsely claiming benefits)
  • A government official can defraud the public (corruption)
Why It Is Different From Just "Stealing" or Just "Lying"

This is an important distinction that sharpens your understanding:

  • Stealing (theft) — You take something by force or sneaking, without the victim's knowledge or consent. A pickpocket steals. A burglar steals. The victim never chose to give anything.
  • Lying — You say something false. But if nothing of value is taken from anyone, it is not defrauding. You might lie to avoid embarrassment, for example, and that alone is not defrauding.
  • Defrauding — The victim actually hands over something (money, rights, property), but only because you manipulated their understanding of reality. Their consent is technically present, but it is manufactured through deception — so it is not genuine, informed consent. This is what makes defrauding particularly serious: you weaponised their trust.

Think of it this way: a thief bypasses your decision; a person who defrauds you corrupts your decision.
The Legal Weight of the Word

"Defraud" is firmly a legal term. It describes a criminal and/or civil offence. When someone is said to have defrauded another:

  • It implies criminal wrongdoing, not just bad behaviour
  • The person who did it (the defrauder) can be prosecuted, fined, and imprisoned
  • The victim may be entitled to compensation through civil courts
  • It is taken seriously because it involves a deliberate, planned act — not a reckless accident

This is why the word is almost always used in serious, formal, or legal contexts. You would find it in court documents, news reports about crimes, and legal statutes — not in casual conversation where someone might simply say "scam," "con," or "cheat."
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

"Defraud" is almost always followed by a person or organisation (the victim), often introduced by the word "of" to indicate what was taken:

  • "He defrauded the bank of millions of dollars."
  • "She was convicted of defrauding elderly people of their savings."
  • "The company defrauded its shareholders of their investments."
  • "He was charged with defrauding the government." (Here, "of" is simply omitted, but implied)

You may also see it used in passive form:

  • "Thousands of customers were defrauded."
  • "She had been defrauded by her own financial adviser."

If you had to remember just one thing:

To defraud someone is to deliberately deceive them so that they lose something of value — while you gain from their loss.

Everything else in this explanation is simply a fuller, richer description of that single idea.
